Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Darkness: Dark spaces, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Michael is a sixty-three-year-old financial analyst who lives with his wife in a quiet suburban neighborhood, a life he once considered stable and predictable. That stability ended on a rainy November evening nine months ago, when he was driving home from a late meeting. The highway was slick, visibility poor, and as he rounded a curve, a delivery truck drifted into his lane. He swerved, but the impact was violent—his sedan spun across three lanes before slamming into a concrete barrier. The car crumpled around him, pinning his legs, and for what felt like an eternity he was trapped in the dark, the smell of gasoline and hot metal filling the cabin, the sound of his own breathing and the hiss of steam from the ruined engine the only things he could hear. He remembers thinking, *This is it. This is how I die.* Rescue workers eventually cut him free, and physically he recovered with only minor injuries. But something inside him had changed.

In the weeks that followed, Michael found that certain smells could undo him entirely. The faint odor of gasoline at a service station would hit him without warning, and suddenly he was back in the crushed car, his chest tight, his hands trembling. He began to avoid filling up his own car, asking his wife to do it instead. Darkness, too, became a problem. He started leaving lights on throughout the house at night—hallways, bathrooms, the kitchen—because the moment he stepped into a dim room, his body would react before his mind had a chance to catch up. His heart would pound, his palms would sweat, and he would feel a surge of adrenaline that made no sense but felt entirely real. Car sounds became the worst of all. The rumble of a truck accelerating, the screech of tires, even the hum of traffic from the street outside his home—each could trigger a vivid auditory recall, the screech of metal and the hiss of steam flooding back into his ears as if it were happening right now. He had come to believe that if he let himself think about the accident, truly think about it, he would not be able to handle it. So he pushed the memories away, distracted himself with work, with television, with anything that kept his mind occupied.

But the vigilance never stopped. He found himself scanning for exits the moment he entered any room or building—restaurants, grocery stores, even his own office. He would note the nearest door, the windows, the path to the parking lot, always calculating an escape route. At night, he would wake suddenly, his body alert, and lie in the dark listening, checking that everything was safe before he could drift back to sleep. He had become convinced that he had to be on guard all the time, because you never know what can happen next. The world, once ordinary, now felt full of hidden dangers.

His wife noticed the changes. He had stopped driving on highways, taking longer surface streets to work, which made him late more often than not. He had snapped at her when she suggested they take a weekend trip, saying he couldn't be in a car that long. She did not understand why he had become so jumpy, so withdrawn. He could not explain it to her—he could barely explain it to himself. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at his desk, when a coworker returned from lunch with the faint smell of diesel on his jacket. Michael had frozen, his vision blurring, his hands gripping the edge of his desk as the memory surged back without warning, felt not as a recollection but as something happening in that very moment. He excused himself to the bathroom and stood there, shaking, staring at his own face in the mirror. He realized he could not keep living like this. He was afraid of what might happen if he let the memories in, but he was more afraid of what was happening to his life—his marriage, his work, his sense of himself. He hoped, more than he could say, that talking about it would not break him.
